definition: For an item that must persist, change, or disappear consistently across MULTIPLE independently-authored cinematics spanning a long in-game timeline (a costume, a stowed prop, a physical state change), maintain one explicit, shared continuity record (the production's own example: a lead animator's map of every costume every actor wears, across time) that every relevant scene is checked against — rather than trusting each scene's own animator to independently remember and maintain consistency.
purpose: Prevent the specific, named failure mode of a state that should persist (or change on a schedule) silently reverting or vanishing because each cinematic referencing it was authored somewhat independently, often by different people, at different times.
visible_effect: Without this discipline, an item that should be present, absent, or in a specific state in a given scene is found to be wrong only when someone happens to notice (the production's own named example: a prop that should have persisted across several missions had simply vanished from a later scene once an unrelated asset update landed).
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: A silent continuity break is invisible until a player or reviewer catches it, at which point it reads as an embarrassing, avoidable inconsistency rather than a deliberate choice — the entire point of the discipline is to catch it before that happens.
physical_interpretation: None — a production/continuity-tracking discipline, not a property of any single motion or scene.
use_cases: any state (costume, held prop, injury, physical change) that must persist, evolve, or be removed consistently across many independently-authored scenes spanning a long narrative timeline

a production where different scenes referencing the same continuity state are assigned to different animators or authored at different times, removing any single person's ability to track it from memory
non_use_cases: a state fully local to one scene with no cross-scene persistence requirement at all, where a shared continuity record would be pure overhead

a small enough production/timeline that one person can reliably track every persistent state from memory without a dedicated record — the discipline scales specifically with the number of scenes and authors, not with complexity alone
interactions: action_end_pose_must_match_idle_for_automatic_blend (W04) — a related but narrower continuity concern (pose continuity across an automatic blend WITHIN one character's state machine) versus this entry's broader concern (a declared item/state's continuity across many independently-authored SCENES)

`ai/library.js`'s cross-project motion library (this build) — the closest existing Cadence mechanism for something persisting and being referenced across multiple otherwise-independent projects, though it stores reusable MOTION, not a continuity STATE record
cadence_representation: Not represented: Cadence's project model is per-`.cadence`-file (CLAUDE.md), with `ai/memory.js project_conventions` as the closest existing mechanism for a fact that should apply consistently across a project's own scenes — but nothing in this build extends that concept ACROSS separate project files the way this entry's continuity record spans many independently-authored cinematics. `ai/library.js` is explicitly the one cross-project store this build has, but it holds reusable motion clips, not a declared state-over-time record for an item like a costume.
control_surface: None. `ai/memory.js project_conventions` could in principle hold a within-project note about item continuity; nothing extends that across separate `.cadence` files.
detection_and_measurement_methods: None — whether an item's presence/state in one project is CONSISTENT with its state in another, separately-authored project is not a question any tool in this build could answer, since nothing links or compares state across separate project files at all.
failure_modes: relying on individual animators' memory for a state that spans many scenes and enough time that no single person can reliably track it, the exact failure this entry's example describes

creating a continuity record but not re-checking it after a LATER, unrelated change (an asset update, a re-authored earlier scene) — the record itself does not prevent drift unless something actively re-validates against it, which is exactly why the same production also introduced a recurring cross-department meeting on top of the record itself
roblox_considerations: None specific — a production/continuity discipline independent of target engine.
examples: a lead animator (Gavin Goulden) building an explicit map of every costume every actor wears across the game's timeline, described directly as a response to a costume/prop continuity break the team had already shipped in an earlier build (video @ 19:33–19:53)

the specific named incident that motivated it: a spider prop meant to persist across several missions and cinematics 'simply vanished' from a later scene once a different department's unrelated asset update landed (video @ 19:11–19:33)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/r_rJJyIPrmM @ 19:11–19:53 — Brian Weiser describes the specific continuity failure and the resulting explicit tracking discipline, crediting lead animator Gavin Goulden by name; no frames extracted (transcript-only); experimental until validated
